lectures.title: The Preamble: source, text, keywords and judicial status

items: **Objectives Resolution:** the Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by **Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru** on **13 December 1946** and adopted on **22 January 1947**.
**Idea of the Preamble:** borrowed from the Constitution of the **USA**.
**Language of the Preamble:** influenced by the **Australian** Constitution.
**Opening:** WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a **SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC** and to secure to all its citizens:
**LIBERTY** of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
**FRATERNITY:** and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;
**Closing:** IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
**Date mentioned in the Preamble:** **26 November 1949** (Date of Adoption).
Supreme authority; free from external control
Added by 42nd Amendment (1976); aims at reducing inequality
Added by 42nd Amendment (1976); equal respect to all religions
Government of the people, by the people, for the people
Head of the State is elected (not hereditary)
Of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
Assuring dignity of individual + unity & integrity of the Nation
**Three types of Justice:** Social, Economic and Political.
**"Federal":** the word “Federal” is not mentioned in the Preamble.
**42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (Mini Constitution):** added three words: **Socialist, Secular, Integrity**.
**Change of phrase:** the 42nd Amendment changed “Unity of the Nation” → “Unity and Integrity of the Nation”.
**Not original:** the words “Socialist” and “Secular” were not originally present.
**Amended only once:** the Preamble has been amended only once so far.
**Article 368:** the Preamble can be amended under Article 368, but the Basic Structure cannot be altered.

parts.t: Judicial status: is the Preamble part of the Constitution?
items: Preamble is NOT a part (not an integral part) of the Constitution; linked Article 3 / Preamble
Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be amended, but Basic Structure cannot be destroyed
Affirmed that the Preamble IS an integral part of the Constitution
Reaffirmed that Preamble is an integral part
**Berubari overturned:** the Berubari Union Case (1960) holding was later overturned by Kesavananda Bharati and S.R. Bommai.
**Preamble status:** Berubari (1960) held the Preamble is NOT part; Kesavananda (1973) and Bommai (1994) held it IS an integral part of the Constitution (settled in Kesavananda Bharati).

parts.t: Nature and significance of the Preamble
items: **Names:** the Preamble is the key to the Constitution / Soul of the Constitution / **Political Horoscope (K.M. Munshi)**.
**Non-justiciable:** it cannot be enforced in a court of law.
**Reflects:** the philosophy, ideals and objectives of the Constitution.
**No power or right:** the Preamble does not confer any power or create any right by itself.

lectures.title: Fundamental Rights: Part III, classification and articles

parts.t: Origin and basics of Fundamental Rights
items: **Part III:** Fundamental Rights are in Part III of the Constitution, **Articles 12 to 35**; total Articles in Part III: **24** (12 to 35).
**Borrowed from:** mainly the **Bill of Rights of the USA**.
**First explicit demand for Fundamental Rights:** Constitution of India Bill, 1895 (Swaraj Bill, 1895).
**Line of demand:** Swaraj Bill (1895) → Motilal Nehru Report (1928) → Karachi Session of Congress (1931).
**Originally 7, now 6:** originally provided 7 Fundamental Rights; presently available 6 Fundamental Rights.
**Right removed:** Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978** and made a legal right under **Article 300-A**.
**First Fundamental Right enforced:** Right to Equality.
**Against the State:** Fundamental Rights are available against the State (Art. 12 defines State).
**Only to citizens:** 5 rights are available only to citizens (Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30).
**Citizens and foreigners:** the rest of the rights are available to both citizens and foreigners (Arts. 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25–28).
**Amendment:** Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but cannot destroy the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
**Guardian of Fundamental Rights:** Judiciary (Supreme Court & High Courts).
Equality before law, prohibition of discrimination, equality of opportunity, abolition of untouchability & titles
Six freedoms; protection in respect of conviction; life & personal liberty; protection against arrest
Prohibition of traffic in human beings & forced labour; prohibition of employment of children in factories
Freedom of conscience, free profession, practice & propagation of religion
Protection of interests of minorities; right of minorities to establish & administer educational institutions
Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
**Six freedoms of the Right to Freedom:** speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession.

parts.t: Articles 12–13 and the Right to Equality (Arts. 14–18)
items: Laws inconsistent with FR void + Judicial Review
Prohibition of discrimination + special provisions (15(4) by 1st Amendment)
Equality of opportunity in public employment + reservation (16(4), 16(4A))
**Article 15(1):** no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth.
**Art. 19:** Six freedoms (19(1)(a)–(g)). Note: 19(1)(f) – Right to Property was deleted.
**Reasonable restrictions under Art. 19:** grounds are 8 (for speech), 3–4 for others.
**Art. 20:** Protection in respect of conviction for offences.
**Art. 21:** Protection of life and personal liberty.
**Art. 21-A:** Right to Education, made a Fundamental Right (added) by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
**Art. 22:** Protection against arrest and detention; maximum period of preventive detention without advisory board: **3 months**.

parts.t: Rights against Exploitation and to Freedom of Religion
items: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
Prohibition of employment of children in factories etc.
Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
Freedom from payment of taxes for promotion of any religion
Freedom from attending religious instruction in certain educational institutions
**Child labour:** prohibited under Art. 24; age below which child labour is prohibited: **14 years**.

parts.t: Cultural and Educational Rights, Remedies and Arts. 33–35
items: **Art. 30:** Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
**Art. 32:** Right to Constitutional Remedies; Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
**Art. 32** was called the **“Heart and Soul” of the Constitution** by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**.
**Arts. 33–35:** Power to modify FR for forces, etc.
No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
Equality of opportunity in public employment
**Art. 358:** Art. 19 is automatically suspended under Art. 358, only in case of War / External Aggression.
**Art. 359:** the President can suspend enforcement of other FRs (except Arts. 20 & 21) by Presidential Order under Art. 359.
**National Emergency:** Fundamental Rights can be suspended during National Emergency (except Arts. 20 & 21 after 44th Amendment).

lectures.title: Fundamental Rights: the five writs under Articles 32 and 226

items: **Constitutional basis:** writs are prerogative remedies borrowed from English common law; issued by the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226).
**5 types of Writs:** Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto.

**Heart and Soul of the Constitution:** Dr. B.R. Ambedkar designated Article 32 as the "heart and soul of the Constitution" because it guarantees a direct, effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies.
**Article 32(3):** Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within its local jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court.

parts.t: Supreme Court and High Courts: scope compared
items: **Supreme Court (Art. 32):** narrower jurisdiction; issues writs ONLY for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Part III).
**High Courts (Art. 226):** wider jurisdiction (wider power); issue writs for Fundamental Rights AND for any other purpose (enforcement of ordinary statutory/legal rights).
**Scope comparison (universal trap):** Supreme Court only for Fundamental Rights (Art. 32); High Courts for Fundamental Rights + other purposes (Art. 226).

parts.t: The five writs: meaning and purpose
items: "To have the body" / "Let us have the body"
Release a person from unlawful/illegal physical detention; safeguards individual liberty
Compel performance of a mandatory public or legal duty that has been refused/neglected
Prevent an inferior court/tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction or usurping jurisdiction not vested in it
Quash an illegal order already passed due to lack/excess of jurisdiction or error of law on the face of the record
Prevent illegal usurpation of a permanent public office created by statute/Constitution
**Habeas Corpus:** quashes illegal or unlawful physical detention.
**Mandamus:** directs a public official, inferior court, or statutory authority to perform a mandatory public/legal duty.
**Prohibition:** issued by a higher court to a lower court, to prevent an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction (preventive).
**Certiorari:** issued by a higher court to quash an order already passed by an inferior court/tribunal due to lack of jurisdiction or error of law (curative and preventive).
**Quo-Warranto:** inquires into the legality of a person's claim to a public office to prevent illegal usurpation.

parts.t: Against whom each writ lies, and at what stage
items: Applicable whenever detention is illegal; can lie against private persons
Public officials, Statutory bodies, Inferior Courts, Tribunals, Government
Does NOT lie against purely private bodies (unless discharging public duty) or President/Governors
Preventive stage: issued while the proceeding is still pending in the lower body
Curative stage: issued after an order/decision is made ("postmortem" review)
Person holding or claiming a substantive public office
Can be moved by any public-minded citizen (does not require aggrieved party status)
**Prohibition:** issued to PREVENT; operates while the judicial/quasi-judicial proceeding is pending to halt excess of jurisdiction.
**Certiorari:** issued to CORRECT/QUASH; operates after the order has been passed to remove or quash decisions suffering from jurisdictional error.
**Habeas Corpus** targets illegal custody of a Person (remedy for bodily freedom).
**Mandamus** targets non-performance of a Legal Duty by a public authority.
**Quo-Warranto** challenges: "Show your legal qualification/title to hold this public office."
**Private individuals:** Habeas Corpus is the only writ directly applicable against private individuals in cases of illegal confinement.
**Government companies (IAS trap):** Mandamus can lie against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function.
**Locus standi exception:** in Quo-Warranto, any member of the public can file a petition (traditional locus standi is relaxed; the petitioner does not need to be personally aggrieved).

lectures.title: Fundamental Rights: landmark cases, doctrines and Rule of Law

items: FRs prevail over DPSPs; reservation validity
Parliament can amend FRs but not Basic Structure
Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right

parts.t: Article 21: from A.K. Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi
items: **A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950):** narrow interpretation of Article 21; focused on "procedure established by law" concerning preventive detention. Linked: Article 21.
**Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978):** widened (expanded) Article 21 (Personal Liberty / Right to Travel Abroad); procedure must be "just, fair, and reasonable".
**Golden triangle:** Maneka Gandhi established that Arts. 14, 19, and 21 are mutually inclusive. Linked Articles 14, 19, 21.
**Procedure Established by Law (Art. 21 text):** law is valid if enacted following correct legislative procedure (A.K. Gopalan, 1950).
**Due Process of Law (Post-Maneka Gandhi, 1978):** law must also be "just, fair, and reasonable" and free from procedural arbitrariness.
**Capital punishment (Bachan Singh):** death penalty in the "rarest of rare cases" is NOT unconstitutional under Article 21.
**K.S. Puttaswamy (2017):** a 9-Judge Bench held Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right. Linked: Article 21 / Part III.

**Champakam Dorairajan (1951):** held that in case of conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs; led directly to the 1st Constitutional Amendment, 1951 (inserted Art. 15(4) for reservations). Linked Articles 15, 29, 37, 46.
**Indra Sawhney (1992):** upheld 27% OBC reservation; creamy layer excluded; capped total reservations at the 50% ceiling (50% vertical limit established). Linked Articles 15(4), 16(4).
**Equal Pay for Equal Work:** delineated in Randhir Singh (1982) by reading Articles 14, 16, and 39(d) with the Preamble.
**Navtej Singh Johar (2018):** decriminalized consensual adult same-sex acts; read down Section 377 IPC. Linked Articles 14, 15, 19, 21.
**Section 377 IPC vs Article 377:** Navtej Singh Johar invalidated provisions of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, NOT Article 377 of the Constitution.

**Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (Shaheen Bagh, 2020):** on youth agitations & public protest; recognized the right to protest peacefully under Article 19, but held that public ways and spaces cannot be occupied indefinitely.
A.K. Gopalan (1950) / State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
Only the offending/unconstitutional portion of a statute is declared void, leaving the valid rest intact if they can be separated.
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955)
Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not dead ab initio; they remain eclipsed.
**Doctrine of Eclipse:** such laws remain overshadowed/dormant (eclipsed) and become active if the FR is amended.
**Constitutional anchor in India:** Rule of Law is anchored primarily in Article 14 (Equality before Law and Equal Protection of the Laws), applying to both citizens and foreigners.
**Basic Structure:** Rule of Law is affirmed as part of the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973 & Indira Nehru Gandhi, 1975).
**Equality Before Law:** British origin; negative concept (absence of special privilege for any individual).
**Equal Protection of the Laws:** American origin; positive concept (equal treatment under equal circumstances / Reasonable Classification permitted).
**Arbitrary discretion:** a law that confers on an executive authority an unguided, uncontrolled, and uncanalized discretionary power in the matter of application or enforcement violates Article 14.
**Effect:** such a law violates the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and directly subverts the Rule of Law.
**Administrative Discretion Rule:** executive discretion without objective standards or judicial safeguards is ultra vires Article 14.
